title: The Gold Rush

evidence.note: A full-text search of the Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures volumes for Jan-Dec 1952, Jan-Dec 1953 and Jan-Dec 1954 (archive.org — the complete 1909-Act 28th-year renewal window for a 1925 publication) found no genuine renewal for 'The Gold Rush' in any of the three years; the only hits were unrelated works that happen to mention a historical 'gold rush' (a Lotta Crabtree biographical musical; a documentary on California history). If genuinely never renewed, the real free date is a 28-year non-renewal lapse around 1954.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures, Jan-Dec 1952 / 1953 / 1954 (archive.org)

evidence.note: Independently of the renewal question above: released June 26, 1925 by United Artists; the 95-year US copyright term ceiling for any 1925 work (renewed or not) has expired, so the print is public domain in the US by 1 January 2021 at the very latest regardless of how it got there.

The 1925 original is silent, so its images are free. The 1942 reissue added a recorded musical score and Chaplin's narration, and that score earned Academy Award nominations for Max Terr (music) and James L. Fields (sound). Any score or narration on a modern copy is a separate work and cannot be assumed free.
An original screenplay written by Chaplin and published as the 1925 film. It is not an adaptation of an earlier work, so it shares the film's expired 1925 term.

A Criterion Collection Blu-ray (2012) pairs a 1925 reconstruction with the 1942 narrated version, and a 4K restoration premiered at Cannes in 2025. A faithful restoration adds no new US copyright. New scores, titles or other added material in such releases can be protected, so check what each release adds.

renewal_search.negative_result: No genuine renewal found in a full-text search of the 1952, 1953 and 1954 CCE motion-pictures volumes (see print layer evidence); the film is public domain either way (non-renewal lapse ~1954, or the 95-year ceiling expiring 2021 if it was renewed under a variant title we missed).

editorial:
The Gold Rush is Charlie Chaplin's 1925 silent comedy for United Artists. His Tramp goes to the Klondike, and the film includes the boiled-shoe dinner and the dancing dinner rolls. It premiered on June 26, 1925. The 1925 print is public domain in the US. A direct search of the 1952-1954 Catalog of Copyright Entries motion-pictures volumes found no genuine renewal, so the more likely mechanism is a 28-year non-renewal lapse around 1954; even if a renewal exists under a variant title we missed, the 95-year ceiling for any 1925 work ran out by 1 January 2021 at the latest. The story was an original Chaplin screenplay — not an adaptation of an outside book or play — so it carries no separate source-work term and shares the print's own public-domain status.

The trap is the 1942 reissue. Chaplin added a recorded score and his own narration, and tightened the edit. That score was Oscar-nominated for Max Terr, and it is a separate work from the 1925 film. Modern releases, including the 2012 Criterion Blu-ray and the 2025 4K restoration, may add scores or other material of their own. Use the silent 1925 version, and score it yourself or use a free-to-use recording.
faq: Can I use clips from The Gold Rush in my own video?
Yes for the 1925 silent footage, since the print's term has expired in the US. Avoid the 1942 reissue, which has Chaplin's narration and a recorded score, and avoid any copy with a modern score.
Is the Criterion or 2025 restoration free to copy?

A faithful restoration adds no new US copyright, but added scores, new titles or other material can be protected. Ripping a copy-protected disc may also breach 17 U.S.C. 1201. Use the silent Internet Archive copy instead.
